ocar.opportunity: Connectomics and neuronal diversity make cell-type taxonomies more urgent, but morphology-based classification still depends on computational choices that are hard to compare across papers.
ocar.challenge: Studies differ in algorithms, morphological representations, and evaluation metrics, and many reports fail quality screens, so it is unclear which methods actually work and how they should be judged.
ocar.action: Lobato, Leite, Jacob, and Santana present in Neuroscience (2026) a systematic review of peer-reviewed neuronal morphology classification since 2018, screening 840 papers from five databases (2018–2024) and extracting methods, representations, and evaluation from 35 studies that met predefined quality criteria.
ocar.resolution: Artificial neural networks were the main classifier (21 papers), microscopy-image representations for morphometric features were common (30), and accuracy was the dominant metric (29). The authors conclude that no single method is universally superior; effectiveness depends on neuronal type, representation, and features.
ocar.future_work: They point to lessons-learned and future-directions sections and released supplementary material; remaining barriers they flag in the introduction include classifying types, integrating multimodal data, and standardizing connectomics at wider scale.

summaries.beginner: Computers try to sort neurons by shape, but papers use many different recipes. This review of recent studies finds that neural networks and microscope pictures are now the usual tools, and that accuracy scores dominate how those tools are judged.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuroscience (2026), Lobato and colleagues systematically review in silico neuronal morphology classification. From 840 papers (2018–2024) they retained 35 after a risk-of-bias screen. Artificial neural networks classified morphometric features in 21 included papers; image-based representations appeared in 30; accuracy was the evaluation measure in 29. Deep learning is described as popular for automatic feature extraction, yet the authors emphasize that method choice should track neuron type and representation rather than a single winner.
summaries.advanced: Inclusion is 35 of 840, so quantitative counts (21/30/29) describe the quality-filtered set, not the full literature. Accuracy as the dominant metric is itself a limitation the review documents rather than a claim of biological validity. The extract’s introduction is truncated before a full methods recap; conclusions state no universally superior approach. This is a methods review, not a new classifier or connectome.

plain_language_summary: Computers try to sort neurons by shape, but papers use many different recipes. This review of recent studies finds that neural networks and microscope pictures are now the usual tools, and that accuracy scores dominate how those tools are judged.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain recordings show who is active, but not who influences whom on which timescale, especially when dynamics are nonlinear and stimuli change.
ocar.challenge: Pairwise analyses mix lags, parametric transition models are usually assumed, and C. elegans imaging is sampled too slowly to split sub-250 ms events from one-step transitions.
ocar.action: Kinger, Bertram, Dyballa, Yemini, and Zucker introduce Score–Block Time Graphs (SBTG) in an arXiv preprint (2026): denoising score models on joint activity windows, converted via cross-block score products into calibrated, lag-specific directed edge tests, applied to whole-brain C. elegans calcium imaging.
ocar.resolution: SBTG is intended to recover lag-specific circuit structure, including better alignment with independent connectomes, cell-type temporal organization, and neuromodulatory lag profiles. At lag 1 it improves rank alignment with anatomy versus correlation; onset/offset phases shift coupling to longer lags, while sustained stimulation concentrates coupling at short latency.
ocar.future_work: The authors bound interpretation by 4 Hz sampling, coverage of 189 head and 42 tail neurons of 302, lag-dependent power loss, incomplete connectome references, and an identification theorem that requires additive-noise dynamics.

summaries.beginner: Brain recordings show which cells light up, not who is driving whom a moment later. This team turns a machine-learning score of activity snapshots into statistical tests for directed, time-lagged links in the worm C. elegans.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2026 arXiv preprint (2605.02852), Kinger and colleagues present SBTG, which estimates joint-window scores over consecutive brain states and converts cross-block score products into lag-resolved directed edge tests. The identification claim is that those products recover the Jacobian of the transition map under additive-noise dynamics. Applied to C. elegans calcium imaging, they report improved anatomical rank alignment at lag 1, phase-dependent lag structure, and transmitter-specific lag profiles (monoamines and metabotropic signaling aligning at longer lags than faster synaptic systems). Statistical machinery includes cross-fitting, HAC errors, and BY control.
summaries.advanced: Venue is an arXiv preprint, not a journal. Sampling at 4 Hz cannot resolve sub-250 ms mechanisms. Couplings use 189 head plus 42 tail neurons, so hidden-unit bias remains. Power falls with lag as window dimension grows. Theorem 4.1’s exact Jacobian reading requires additive noise and stated stationarity/moment conditions; otherwise SBTG is a reduced-form effective coupling. External Cook/Randi/Bentley connectomes are incomplete proxies for effective connectivity.

plain_language_summary: Brain recordings show which cells light up, not who is driving whom a moment later. This team turns a machine-learning score of activity snapshots into statistical tests for directed, time-lagged links in the worm C. elegans.

ocar.opportunity: Connectome-constrained models can match behavior without using biology-like internal codes, so a population geometry test is needed that does not require a behavioral decoder.
ocar.challenge: Behavioral fidelity is not biological fidelity, as illustrated by a worm connectome trained to produce fly walking, and a published T4/T5 tuning reference collapses to circular structure on ON-edge stimuli.
ocar.action: Zhou and Hasler, on bioRxiv (2026), apply representational similarity analysis and centered kernel alignment to 50 Flyvis connectome-constrained Drosophila visual-system networks versus 50 stability-constrained random baselines (sign-preserving weight shuffles).
ocar.resolution: Connectome-constrained networks produce smoother circular direction geometry than random networks: RSA Spearman r = 0.686 (ON edges) and r = 0.846 (ON+OFF), both p < 0.0001, with CKA p < 0.05 in both experiments. A high r means a more resolved version of structure the random baseline only approximates, not interchangeability.
ocar.future_work: They propose applying the same RSA framework to MICrONS mouse V1. Untrained Flyvis responses sit below float32 resolution, so a trained-versus-untrained wiring-prior test is left unresolved; a matched experimental reference and better-conditioned whitened RDMs are also needed.

summaries.beginner: A model can walk like a fly without thinking like a fly. This paper measures the shape of population responses in fruit-fly visual networks and finds that real wiring makes a cleaner circular map of motion direction than shuffled wiring.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2026), Zhou and Hasler propose representational geometry as a fidelity metric for connectome-constrained networks, using RSA and CKA on the Flyvis Drosophila visual-system ensemble (n = 50) versus stability-constrained random shuffles (n = 50). RSA Spearman correlations of connectome-constrained versus random geometry are r = 0.686 for ON edges and r = 0.846 for ON+OFF (p < 0.0001). Comparison to a Maisak et al. (2013) T4/T5 reference is judged uninterpretable on ON-only stimuli because the reference reduces to four equal-width cardinal tunings. Residual CC advantage after circular control (0.145 vs 0.061) is not significant at n = 50.
summaries.advanced: All analyses use one pretrained Flyvis ensemble on one optic-flow task. Experiment 3’s biological reference is confounded by circular stimulus structure. Whitened RDMs have condition numbers ~10^7. Untrained networks cannot yield RDMs because responses fall below float32 round-off; 8.1% of cell-type pairs are silenced by Flyvis’s non-negativity clamp at small perturbation. The MICrONS extension is proposed, not run. Catalog tags list C. elegans; the study is Drosophila visual system (C. elegans appears only as Brunton et al.’s counterexample).

plain_language_summary: A model can walk like a fly without thinking like a fly. This paper measures the shape of population responses in fruit-fly visual networks and finds that real wiring makes a cleaner circular map of motion direction than shuffled wiring.

ocar.opportunity: If simple neuron statistics carry species-specific design signatures, comparative connectomics could skip expensive deep models and still recover phylogenetic structure.
ocar.challenge: Datasets differ in completeness, annotation, and reconstruction, so missing-value imputation and class imbalance can be mistaken for biology.
ocar.action: Kawada, at the 14th International Conference on Bioinformatics and Computational Biology (2026), unifies eight electron-microscopy reconstructions spanning five species (N = 176,914 neurons) and classifies species from cable length, synapse count, and synaptic partner count with a random forest, using SHAP and a two-pipeline complete-case versus imputation design.
ocar.resolution: The random forest reached 92.2% accuracy versus a 60.7% linear baseline (McNemar χ² = 9153.78, p < 10⁻⁴). SHAP showed opposite length effects (negative for zebrafish, positive for mouse). Imputing missing local density raised feature importance by 76.9%. In C. elegans, unsupervised clustering found subpopulations with opposing wiring rules, described as a decoupled length–synapse signature.
ocar.future_work: The paper’s stated standards are imputation-aware pipelines and mean per-class recall instead of raw accuracy on imbalanced data; applying those standards to newer, more complete reconstructions is the implied next step.

summaries.beginner: Different animals’ neurons might have simple numerical fingerprints. Using three measurements—cable length, synapse count, and partner count—this study trains a classifier that mostly tells species apart, while warning that filling in missing values can fake a biological story.
summaries.intermediate: At ICBCB (2026), Kawada reports a cross-species analysis of eight EM reconstructions and 176,914 neurons over roughly 500 million years of evolution. A random forest on three low-dimensional features reached 92.2% accuracy versus 60.7% for a linear baseline. SHAP attributed opposite neurite-length effects to zebrafish versus mouse. Imputing missing local density increased that feature’s importance by 76.9%, motivating a complete-case versus imputation split. Unsupervised clustering in C. elegans is described as revealing conflicting wiring rules hidden by a global length–synapse independence.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF extract jumps from the abstract into a two-column IEEE layout and then to conclusions/references, so quantitative claims are those in the abstract and closing biological paragraph. “First large-scale” is an authorship claim. 92.2% accuracy is on severely imbalanced species labels; the author argues mean per-class recall should be primary. SHAP effects are correlative species discriminants, not proven evolutionary mechanisms. N = 176,914 pools heterogeneous reconstructions.

plain_language_summary: Different animals’ neurons might have simple numerical fingerprints. Using three measurements—cable length, synapse count, and partner count—this study trains a classifier that mostly tells species apart, while warning that filling in missing values can fake a biological story.

ocar.opportunity: Synapses sit along dendrites and share local resources, so spatial layout might be an extra stabilizer of learning beyond classical temporal Hebbian rules.
ocar.challenge: Testing local co-occupation of weight states needs synapse-scale positions and statistics at once, and static electron microscopy cannot watch plasticity unfold.
ocar.action: Zhu, Chen, Zhao, Xiong, Peng, Wu, and Zhang, on bioRxiv (2026), analyze synaptic weight arrangement in the H01 human temporal-cortex EM connectome (and mouse V1), formalize a center-elevated, surround-suppressed Hebbian model, and port the principle to Spatial Synaptic Regularization (SSR) in artificial networks.
ocar.resolution: Dendritic spines clustered morphologically, while weights showed local elevation with surround suppression; strong synapses lowered the chance that neighbors reached high-weight states. SSR reduced forgetting on continual vision, language-model knowledge editing, and vision-language adapter tasks by preserving high-rank, low-overlap representations. The suppression zone is reported at approximately 10–20 μm.
ocar.future_work: The authors say definitive mechanism tests need dynamic experiments such as in vivo two-photon imaging of weight changes with local Ca²⁺ perturbation; the extract’s limitations paragraph is truncated at “The center-s”.

summaries.beginner: Learning has to add new memories without wiping old ones. This team finds a center-surround pattern of synapse strengths along human cortical dendrites and turns that pattern into a regularizer that helps artificial networks forget less.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2026), Zhu and colleagues analyze the H01 human temporal-cortex EM volume (and mouse V1). Spines clustered morphologically, whereas synaptic weights followed a center-elevated, surround-suppressed layout. A regularized Hebbian model treats a high-weight synapse as lowering neighbors’ probability of also occupying high-weight states. Translating that geometry into SSR is reported to stabilize continual visual learning, LLM knowledge editing, and parameter-efficient vision-language adaptation. Discussion aligns the ~10–20 μm suppression zone with known Ca²⁺ diffusion and dendritic integration scales.
summaries.advanced: Static EM infers a statistical footprint, not observed plasticity; the particle-physics analogy is explicit. SSR success is qualitative in the extract (no numeric forgetting scores here). Mouse V1 is mentioned as a second volume but H01 is the headline dataset. The selected discussion cuts off mid-limitations. Co-potentiation in the immediate vicinity versus inhibition of large neighbors is a selective, not uniform, surround.

plain_language_summary: Learning has to add new memories without wiping old ones. This team finds a center-surround pattern of synapse strengths along human cortical dendrites and turns that pattern into a regularizer that helps artificial networks forget less.

ocar.opportunity: Cerebellar roles now include cognition and affect, but its directed, weighted wiring is still poorly mapped relative to cortex.
ocar.challenge: Intrinsic, extrinsic, lateralized, and interhemispheric projections must be combined from heterogeneous tract-tracing reports without flattening anatomical hierarchy.
ocar.action: Schmitt, Morawska, Prathapan, and Eipert, in The Cerebellum (2026), build a directionally weighted cerebellar subnetwork in neuroVIISAS from a meta-analytic database of over 7,800 high-resolution rat tract-tracing studies, then analyze motifs, modules, hubs, and edge-removal vulnerability.
ocar.resolution: The network has 862 regions and over 21,000 edges and is described as small-world and scale-free at mesoscale, with non-random motifs and functionally coherent modules. Brainstem–cerebellar loops are highlighted as integrative hubs. Removing high-significance edges rapidly degrades clustering relative to rewired surrogates, which the authors read as structurally privileged bottlenecks.
ocar.future_work: They call for multimodal, dynamic, and cross-species extensions that add neuronal dynamics, synaptic plasticity, and gene expression to realize translational cerebellar network models.

summaries.beginner: The cerebellum is more than a motor helper, but its wiring diagram is less mapped than the rest of the brain. This paper assembles thousands of rat tracing studies into a large directed network and looks for hubs and fragile links.
summaries.intermediate: Published in The Cerebellum (2026), Schmitt and colleagues construct a hierarchically organized, directionally weighted rat cerebellar connectome from more than 7,800 tract-tracing studies (862 regions, >21,000 edges), including intrinsic, extrinsic, and interhemispheric projections. Graph analyses report small-world and scale-free mesoscale structure, non-random motifs, and modular subsystems, with hubs concentrated in brainstem–cerebellar loops. A vulnerability analysis finds that deleting high-significance edges collapses clustering faster than in rewired surrogates. Code is pointed to neuroVIISAS.
summaries.advanced: This is a meta-analytic tract-tracing connectome, not a synapse-resolution EM map; “first comprehensive” is an authorship claim. Edge weights are anatomical-significance scores, not synaptic counts. Scale-free/small-world labels are mesoscale graph summaries. The selected extract’s later pages are license and references rather than full numerical tables. Translational claims about health and disease are prospective.

plain_language_summary: The cerebellum is more than a motor helper, but its wiring diagram is less mapped than the rest of the brain. This paper assembles thousands of rat tracing studies into a large directed network and looks for hubs and fragile links.

ocar.opportunity: Human cortical neurons have more elaborate neurites than rodent neurons even after size is accounted for, so morphology itself might explain extra local-circuit complexity.
ocar.challenge: Potential contacts set by axon and dendrite geometry are not the same as synapses, and many formation rules could map potential to actual connectivity.
ocar.action: Barros-Zulaica, Egas Santander, Kanari, Shi, Perin, Pezzoli, Benavides-Piccione, DeFelipe, de Kock, Segev, Markram, and Reimann, on bioRxiv (2026), predict local connectomes from reconstructed human versus rodent morphologies and compare complexity measures, clustering, and synapse-formation scenarios including a Hebbian-compatible process.
ocar.resolution: Connectomes predicted from human morphologies had higher complexity on several functionally relevant measures. The authors argue they show mechanistically how neurite shapes generate non-random clustered structure seen in experiments, and that human shapes strengthen that process. A formation rule compatible with Hebbian plasticity gave the highest complexity and the best match to experimental patterns.
ocar.future_work: How other synapse-formation processes interact with potential connectivity is framed conceptually; the selected extract jumps from a truncated abstract into supplementary figures, so further quantitative tables are not in the extract.

summaries.beginner: Human brain cells are bushier than rodent cells, not just bigger. This study uses those 3D shapes to guess where synapses could form and finds that the human shapes produce more complex local wiring.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2026), Barros-Zulaica and colleagues treat axonal and dendritic geometry as a constraint on potential synaptic contacts in local microcircuitry. Predicted connectomes from human reconstructed morphologies showed higher complexity than rodent counterparts on measures the authors describe as functionally relevant. They further claim a mechanistic account of non-random clustering in experimentally measured connectomes, amplified by human neurite shapes. Among conceptual synapse-formation processes, a Hebbian-compatible rule produced the highest complexity and the closest match to observed patterns.
summaries.advanced: Results are about predicted/potential connectivity, not a measured human EM connectome. The PDF extract’s discussion was not captured (text continues into figure supplements S3–S5). Species comparison depends on the reconstructed morphology set and on how potential contacts are instantiated. “Highest complexity” for the Hebbian-compatible process is stated in the abstract without numeric scores in this extract.

plain_language_summary: Human brain cells are bushier than rodent cells, not just bigger. This study uses those 3D shapes to guess where synapses could form and finds that the human shapes produce more complex local wiring.

ocar.opportunity: Large, well-documented visual connectomes now let synaptic weight histograms be compared across fly and mouse, hinting at shared learning statistics.
ocar.challenge: Lognormal versus power-law reports conflict, and proofreading completeness changes how heavy the tails look.
ocar.action: Cirunay, Papp, and Ódor, on bioRxiv (version posted 30 April 2026), numerically compare global synaptic weights and local node strengths in the mouse visual cortex (including a v1507 proofread snapshot) and the male Drosophila optic lobe, with degree-preserving and random-topology nulls and a generalized-central-limit-theorem argument.
ocar.resolution: Global weights P(w) follow power-law tails with exponents α ≥ 3 (heavy-tailed but finite variance), whereas weights around source and sink neurons fit α < 3. Local strengths P(s) show dual power-law scaling driven mainly by degree heterogeneity; edge-weight correlations were below 1%. Proofreading strongly changes apparent tail heaviness.
ocar.future_work: They caution that finite-size cutoffs can make lognormals look like the right model, and they note that dual-power-law contactome features were set aside as likely structural specifics.

summaries.beginner: Lists of synapse strengths in fly and mouse visual systems look heavy-tailed. This paper argues the whole network follows one kind of tail, while the busiest cells follow a fatter one, and that incomplete proofreading can change the picture.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2026 update of 10.1101/2025.11.10.687553), Cirunay, Papp, and Ódor analyze synaptic weights in mouse visual cortex and the male fruit-fly optic lobe. Global P(w) is reported as power-law with α ≥ 3, while synapses incident on broadcaster/integrator (source/sink) nodes fit α < 3. Node strengths show dual power-law regimes that degree-preserving nulls reproduce but random-topology nulls do not. Weight–weight correlations were <1%, used to justify an approximate CLT/GCLT explanation of why local strengths can look lognormal even if global weights are power-law. Proofreading depth is shown to alter tail heaviness.
summaries.advanced: α thresholds are model fits, not a unique generative proof of criticality. “Most well-documented” is an authorship framing. Dual-power-law (dPL) contactome results are partly set aside. Fly and mouse visual systems are analogized via motion processing, not claimed to share identical circuits. Mouse snapshot v1507 is singled out as most accurate in the discussion of source/sink tails.

plain_language_summary: Lists of synapse strengths in fly and mouse visual systems look heavy-tailed. This paper argues the whole network follows one kind of tail, while the busiest cells follow a fatter one, and that incomplete proofreading can change the picture.

ocar.opportunity: Empirical connectomes show power-law global weights and lognormal node strengths alongside avalanche-like activity, suggesting a shared self-organized critical mechanism.
ocar.challenge: Most discrete models capture avalanches or structure, not both, and they often need fine tuning.
ocar.action: Cirunay, Batac, and Ódor, in Scientific Reports (2025; arXiv:2504.01565), run a continuous sandpile-like avalanche model on hierarchical modular baseline networks with Hebbian edge-weight updates that strengthen co-active links.
ocar.resolution: Avalanche size distributions were robust power laws with a 3/2 exponent on toppled-site counts, matching a classical neuronal-avalanche signature. Hebbian learning recovered power-law edge-weight tails near exponent 3 and lognormal node-degree statistics comparable to connectome data. Homogeneous 4D lattice controls did not yield equally clear power laws, implicating modularity.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the combination of hierarchical modular wiring plus adaptive weights as a balanced SOC account; they note remaining questions about parameter robustness and relation to mean-field exponent 3.

summaries.beginner: Real brain networks have heavy-tailed connection strengths and bursty activity. This model lets pretend neurons avalanche on a modular web and strengthen links when they fire together, reproducing both kinds of statistics without hand-tuning a critical point.
summaries.intermediate: In Scientific Reports (2025), Cirunay, Batac, and Ódor place a continuous sandpile process on hierarchical modular networks and add Hebbian weight updates. They report robust power-law avalanche-size distributions, with toppled-site counts fitted by the 3/2 exponent associated with neuronal avalanches, across network sizes and initial wiring probabilities tested. Edge-weight tails are fitted by decaying power laws near exponent 3, and node degrees by lognormals, compared with empirical connectomes. Discussion attributes robustness to SOC mean-field universality for d > dc = 3 and to modular rare-region/Griffiths effects.
summaries.advanced: The extract is the arXiv layout of the same titled paper as the Scientific Reports DOI. Exponent 3/2 and ~3 are reported as best fits, not unique proofs of a critical brain. Comparisons to “actual connectomes” are qualitative in the extract (figures cited, numbers not tabulated here). Baseline HMNs mimic circuitry; they are not EM reconstructions. Preliminary 4D lattice controls are described as not providing clear power laws.

plain_language_summary: Real brain networks have heavy-tailed connection strengths and bursty activity. This model lets pretend neurons avalanche on a modular web and strengthen links when they fire together, reproducing both kinds of statistics without hand-tuning a critical point.

ocar.opportunity: A complete Drosophila connectome can be frozen as an echo-state reservoir, testing whether biological topology and weights help chaotic time-series prediction.
ocar.challenge: Full-brain reservoirs are large; neuron-class proportions may or may not matter; standard random reservoirs overfit.
ocar.action: Costi, Hadjiivanov, Dold, Hale, and Izzo, in Biomimetics (2025), build echo-state networks from the fly connectome, subsample the most connected neurons with or without preserving class proportions, add hybrid topology/weight shuffles, and also train a reservoir on the entire connectome.
ocar.resolution: Connectome-based reservoirs were more resilient to overfitting than standard implementations, especially in already overfitting regimes. Hybrids showed that both topology and synaptic weights contribute. Using the entire connectome, despite more trained readout parameters, remained overfitting-resilient and reached a normalized error under 2% at lower regularization than the other reservoirs trained with higher regularization.
ocar.future_work: The authors propose other biologically plausible cell-selection rules, tests on other species’ full connectomes, and physical neuromorphic or organoid implementations.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly wiring can be used as a fixed computer network that only trains a thin readout. This study finds that real fly topology and synapse weights resist overfitting better than typical random reservoirs on chaotic time-series tasks.
summaries.intermediate: In Biomimetics (2025), Costi and colleagues turn the documented Drosophila connectome into echo-state connectivity matrices. They compare class-preserving versus class-breaking selection of the most connected neurons, hybrids with connectome topology plus random weights or vice versa, and a full-connectome reservoir. Connectome architecture is reported as significantly more overfitting-resilient than state-of-the-art random reservoirs. The full-brain reservoir kept a normalized error under 2% at lower regularization. Code is at a European Space Agency GitLab repository.
summaries.advanced: The task is multivariate chaotic time-series prediction, not fly behavior. “Significantly more resilient” is stated without a specific test statistic in the extract. The under-2% error is for the entire-connectome condition at lower regularization, not a universal score. Whether overfitting resilience is a general property of biological brains is explicitly a hypothesis. Neuron-class metadata come from the documented connectome release used by the authors.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly wiring can be used as a fixed computer network that only trains a thin readout. This study finds that real fly topology and synapse weights resist overfitting better than typical random reservoirs on chaotic time-series tasks.

ocar.opportunity: Non-random synaptic motifs are hard to lesion in tissue but can be rewritten in large biophysically detailed simulations to test causation.
ocar.challenge: Ad-hoc rewiring must preserve pathway physiology, dendritic innervation patterns, and SONATA-scale models while fitting stochastic connectivity of varying complexity.
ocar.action: Pokorny, Awile, Isbister, Kurban, Wolf, and Reimann present Connectome-Manipulator on bioRxiv (2024), a Python framework to create, fit, transplant, and simplify SONATA connectomes, demonstrated on a detailed rat somatosensory-cortex model.
ocar.resolution: Two use cases: transplanting VIP+ interneuron targeting trends from mouse EM data, and replacing excitatory connectivity with simplified stochastic models of increasing order. After firing-rate recalibration, they report diverse, population-specific activity shifts causally linked to the manipulations, including changes in external versus internal drive related to missing excitatory synapses.
ocar.future_work: The discussion frames the tool as making systematic, reproducible structure–function experiments feasible; the extract notes that ad-hoc scripts could in principle do the same jobs but would re-solve fitting, physiology preservation, and synapse-location reuse.

summaries.beginner: To learn what a wiring pattern does, you need to change it. This software rewires large simulated rat cortex models in a controlled way and shows that those changes shift which cell groups are driven from inside versus outside the network.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2024), Pokorny and colleagues describe Connectome-Manipulator for SONATA network models. It fits stochastic connectivity against existing connectomes and can transplant features or generate simplified instances while preserving pathway synaptic physiology and reusing dendritic synapse locations. In a rat somatosensory model they transplanted VIP+ inhibitory targeting from mouse EM and, separately, rewired excitatory connections with simplified stochastic rules (orders 1–5). Recalibrated spontaneous rates mostly matched in vivo references (an exception is noted for the 2nd-order connectome at PF_R = 1.0). Conductance-injection shifts are related to missing excitatory synapses versus a 1.1 synapses/µm dendritic reference.
summaries.advanced: Causation is inside a morphologically detailed model, not an in vivo lesion. VIP+ trends are transplanted from mouse EM into rat cortex. Figure 6’s quantitative shifts are described qualitatively in the extract (rates, Euclidean rate error, conductance changes) without copying a full table. PF_R is an in vivo fraction parameter in their calibration, not a universal constant. Simplified connectomes are stochastic approximations, not unique biological ground truth.

plain_language_summary: To learn what a wiring pattern does, you need to change it. This software rewires large simulated rat cortex models in a controlled way and shows that those changes shift which cell groups are driven from inside versus outside the network.

ocar.opportunity: A whole-brain fly connectome plus calcium imaging can test whether early taste circuits keep qualities separate or mix them like olfaction.
ocar.challenge: Taste appears distributed across behaviors and brain areas, and labellar gustatory receptor neurons are hard to assign to sweet, water, and related classes from morphology alone.
ocar.action: Li, Dhaliwal, Stanley, Junca, and Gordon, on bioRxiv (2024), combine connectome analysis with functional imaging of early Drosophila taste circuits, focusing on local interneurons postsynaptic to labellar sensory neurons and taste projection neurons (TPNs).
ocar.resolution: Taste quality remained largely segregated in cholinergic and GABAergic LNs. Many TPNs to superior protocerebrum received mainly indirect input via cholinergic LNs, which appear as hubs onto morphologically similar TPN sets. A small sample of representative TPNs still showed mostly segregated taste information.
ocar.future_work: The authors treat GRN typing as imperfect (neurotransmitter prediction; sweet/water left merged) and call for morphological and connectivity studies within classes; they contrast this organization with olfactory PNs that sit directly postsynaptic to receptor neurons.

summaries.beginner: Flies taste sugar, bitter, and more, but it has been unclear how that information is organized in the brain. Combining a wiring diagram with imaging, this team finds that taste types stay mostly separate in the first brain cells, with local neurons acting as hubs to later projection cells.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2024), Li and colleagues analyze early adult Drosophila taste circuitry using the whole-brain connectome and calcium imaging. Cholinergic and GABAergic local interneurons directly postsynaptic to labellar sensory neurons largely preserve taste-quality segregation. Many TPNs receive primarily indirect input through cholinergic LNs that each contact morphologically similar TPN groups. Representative TPN imaging, plus a check that peafowl is taste-responsive, supports mostly segregated information at that level as well. Discussion contrasts this hub-and-third-order architecture with olfactory projection neurons.
summaries.advanced: GRN classification is explicitly uncertain: bitter and Ir94e are morphological, Ppk23glut uses neurotransmitter prediction, and sweet/water are merged unlike Engert et al. and Shiu et al. TPN physiology is described as a small representative set. “Unappreciated logic” is an interpretive headline. The extract cuts off during discussion. Functional claims mix connectome inference with limited imaging, not a full census of TPNs.

plain_language_summary: Flies taste sugar, bitter, and more, but it has been unclear how that information is organized in the brain. Combining a wiring diagram with imaging, this team finds that taste types stay mostly separate in the first brain cells, with local neurons acting as hubs to later projection cells.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans is small enough that structure and physiology could be modeled together if activity and connectome files were in one format.
ocar.challenge: Calcium datasets use different protocols and neuron subsets, and connectomes need preprocessing; labs cannot easily train shared models.
ocar.action: Simeon, Astrom, Kashyap, Kording, and Boyden, in an arXiv preprint (v4, 19 May 2025), compile 12 neuroimaging experiments and 9 connectome annotations from 3 primary EM studies plus a signal-propagation study, with a homogenization pipeline and public Hugging Face/GitHub release.
ocar.resolution: Physiology traces are ordered, resampled, masked, normalized, and smoothed, yielding recordings from approximately 900 worms and 250 uniquely labeled neurons. Connectomes are presented as graphs of the entire nervous system. The resource is aimed at GNNs, state-space models, and structure–function comparison.
ocar.future_work: Limitations they list include calcium imaging, noisy connectomics, and standardization trade-offs; they expect newer imaging to extend the resource toward foundation-style models of small nervous systems.

summaries.beginner: Worm brain data sit in many incompatible files. This project puts calcium recordings and wiring diagrams into one cleaned format so people can study how structure relates to activity.
summaries.intermediate: In arXiv:2411.12091 (v4, 2025), Simeon, Astrom, Kashyap, Kording, and Boyden homogenize 12 C. elegans calcium-fluorescence experiments and connectome annotations from three primary EM reconstructions plus a signal-propagation study (nine annotations). The pipeline standardizes neuron order and sampling rate, producing ~900 worms and ~250 uniquely labeled neurons among the worm’s ~300 cells. Datasets are released on Hugging Face with preprocessing code on GitHub. Discussion flags GNN and SSM use cases and trade-offs of calcium, noisy synapses, and resampling.
summaries.advanced: This is a data-and-code resource, not a new biological finding. Catalog author list omits Hector Astrom, who is on the PDF. “4 primary connectome publications” in the conclusion versus “3 EM + 1 signal-propagation” in the abstract should be read as the same compilation. ~900 worms and ~250 labeled neurons are pipeline outputs, not simultaneous whole-brain coverage in every animal. Preprint, not a journal.

plain_language_summary: Worm brain data sit in many incompatible files. This project puts calcium recordings and wiring diagrams into one cleaned format so people can study how structure relates to activity.

ocar.opportunity: Aggression includes actions shared by both sexes, but most known fly aggression neurons are sexually dimorphic and fruitless-positive.
ocar.challenge: How a monomorphic motor program is implemented, and whether it sits in the same circuit as fru+ aggression neurons, is unclear.
ocar.action: Tao, Ayambem, Barranca, and Bhandawat, in Journal of Neuroscience (2024), activate CL062 neurons in males and females, including isolated and head-fixed animals, and examine connectivity in a female EM dataset relative to known fru+ aggression neurons and descending neurons.
ocar.resolution: CL062, previously tied to male aggression, also elicits female aggression-like actions acutely and without a target; the action set is shared but overall behavior remains sexually dimorphic. CL062 is fru− and, in the female connectome, has limited links to known aggression neurons and contacts different descending neurons, supporting a parallel monomorphic pathway.
ocar.future_work: They contrast CL062 with female aIPg and pC1d (including persistence differences) and argue aggression control is more distributed than a single dimorphic pathway; how CL062 relates to those circuits in behaving animals remains to be tested.

summaries.beginner: Male and female fruit flies both threaten and fight, but most known aggression cells work in only one sex. Activating a small set of neurons called CL062 produces aggression-like movements in both sexes, even with no opponent nearby.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Neuroscience (2024), Tao and colleagues show that CL062 neurons elicit aggression-like actions in Drosophila males and females, including without a target. The same actions appear in both sexes, yet overall behavior is sexually dimorphic and mirrors natural target-directed differences. CL062 does not express fruitless. Female EM connectomics (FAFB-FlyWire acknowledgments) indicate limited connectivity with previously characterized fru+ aggression neurons and distinct descending-neuron outputs, so the authors place CL062 in a monomorphic circuit parallel to known dimorphic pathways.
summaries.advanced: Whether observed actions “are aggression” is argued from kinematics and sequence similarity, not from winning a fight. Connectomic independence is from a female EM dataset and synapse counts to DNs (Figure 13), not a causal circuit break. Parallelism is an interpretation of weak linkage plus fru− identity. Optogenetic activation can drive unnatural intensity; isolation assays remove social context by design.

plain_language_summary: Male and female fruit flies both threaten and fight, but most known aggression cells work in only one sex. Activating a small set of neurons called CL062 produces aggression-like movements in both sexes, even with no opponent nearby.

ocar.opportunity: Millimeter-scale cortical EM contains tens of thousands of cells, most with incomplete arbors, so a cheap perisomatic classifier could target proofreading toward rare types.
ocar.challenge: Standard morphological typing wants near-complete axons or dendrites, and connectivity-defined types (chandelier, basket) usually need axonal proofreading.
ocar.action: Elabbady, Seshamani, Mu, Mahalingam, Schneider-Mizell, and the MICrONS Consortium, on bioRxiv (version posted 13 January 2024), survey somatic, nuclear, and perisomatic synapse features for all cells in a cubic millimeter of mouse cortex and train hierarchical classifiers, with a second thinner volume as a transfer check.
ocar.resolution: The authors report that the perisomatic region is surprisingly sufficient to identify cell types, including some types defined mainly by connectivity, and that this labeling supports cell-type-specific connectivity analysis and search for rare patterns. A second animal’s 50 µm-thick cutout (n = 1,944 somas) preserved similar feature correlations and UMAP separation of layers and classes.
ocar.future_work: Extended-data models using unsupervised Schneider-Mizell subclass labels had lower cross-validation (excitatory 67%, inhibitory 85%) than expert labels, especially among fine layer 4/6 distinctions; full axonal validation is limited in the thin volume.

summaries.beginner: In huge electron-microscope volumes, most neurons are only partly traced. This team shows that measurements around the cell body are often enough to guess the cell type, so rare cells can be found without finishing every axon.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2024 update of 10.1101/2022.07.20.499976), Elabbady and colleagues present a perisomatic feature survey across a cubic millimeter of mouse cortex in the MICrONS EM volume. Quantitative soma, nucleus, and perisomatic-synapse features are used to classify neuronal and non-neuronal types, including some connectivity-defined inhibitory classes, without requiring fully proofread arbors. They argue this enables type-specific connectivity characterization and locating rare connectivity patterns. Extended Data Figure 7 reports similar perisomatic feature structure in a second animal’s 50 µm column (n = 1,944 somas).
summaries.advanced: The selected extract’s main results section is truncated; headline sufficiency is from the abstract, while numeric cross-validation in the extract is for alternative unsupervised subclass labels (67% excitatory / 85% inhibitory), not the expert-label main model. The second dataset cannot fully validate subclasses because axons and dendrites are truncated. “First systematic survey” is an authorship claim. Pericytes were manually excluded in the second volume due to segmentation quality.

plain_language_summary: In huge electron-microscope volumes, most neurons are only partly traced. This team shows that measurements around the cell body are often enough to guess the cell type, so rare cells can be found without finishing every axon.

ocar.opportunity: Cortical assemblies are usually modeled as extra pairwise excitation, while inhibition is treated as untargeted blanket suppression.
ocar.challenge: Pairwise maps can miss higher-order motifs that organize both excitation and inhibition, and a 0.65 mm³ EM volume still truncates long-range axons.
ocar.action: Reimann, Egas Santander, Ecker, and Muller, in Cerebral Cortex (2024), detect directed simplices in the excitatory subgraph of the MICrONS mm³ mouse visual-cortex reconstruction and ask how inhibitory cells attach to sequential positions in those motifs.
ocar.resolution: Excitation was organized as feed-forward flow in large non-random motifs from few sources to more potential targets. Inhibitory neurons contacted specific sequential positions, implementing targeted, symmetrical competition between motifs—structure invisible in pairwise connectivity alone. PTC versus DTC (PV- versus SST-like) simplex targeting differences were largely explained by in- and out-degree, unlike some assembly models.
ocar.future_work: They relate the picture to neural manifolds and to long-range predictions that maximum simplicial dimension would increase if missing axons were restored; overlapping subnetworks mean quantitative variability estimates are not independent.

summaries.beginner: Brain cells are often described as teams that excite each other, with inhibition sprayed on everyone. In a piece of mouse visual cortex, inhibition instead aims at particular places in larger wiring patterns that you cannot see if you only look at pairs of cells.
summaries.intermediate: In Cerebral Cortex (2024), Reimann and colleagues analyze excitation and inhibition in the MICrONS electron-microscopic reconstruction of a 0.65 mm³ mouse visual-cortex volume. Directed simplices in the excitatory network define source-to-target information-flow motifs. Inhibitory neurons synapse onto characteristic sequential positions in those motifs, yielding targeted competition rather than blanket inhibition. None of the reported trends appear in pairwise connectivity alone. Discussion notes that a 300 μm slice would miss ~90% of (cat) excitatory connectivity by a cited estimate, while inhibitory loss is lower when all inhibitory cells are kept.
summaries.advanced: Catalog journal field lists bioRxiv; the PDF is the Cerebral Cortex article (DOI 10.1093/cercor/bhae433). Overlapping subnetworks violate independence for quantitative error bars; presence of structure in every subnetwork is the robustness claim. PV/SST correspondence to PTC/DTC is approximate. Competition here is between groups sharing sources, not classic lateral inhibition between disjoint assemblies. Simplicial dimension and neuron counts of missing long-range axons are partly inferred from a rat S1 model cited as a control.

plain_language_summary: Brain cells are often described as teams that excite each other, with inhibition sprayed on everyone. In a piece of mouse visual cortex, inhibition instead aims at particular places in larger wiring patterns that you cannot see if you only look at pairs of cells.

ocar.opportunity: Cortical synapse censuses need a reliable split between thick-PSD asymmetric (mostly excitatory) and thin-PSD symmetric (mostly inhibitory) contacts in volume EM.
ocar.challenge: Potassium ferrocyanide, used to darken membranes, thins postsynaptic densities and makes symmetric synapses especially hard to call.
ocar.action: Cano-Astorga, Plaza-Alonso, Turégano-López, Rodrigo-Rodríguez, Merchán-Pérez, and DeFelipe, in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2024), describe a FIB-SEM protocol on mouse brain, titrating ferrocyanide and validating symmetric synapses as GABAergic with VGAT immunocytochemistry.
ocar.resolution: A low ferrocyanide concentration (0.1%) improved membrane visualization while still allowing unequivocal AS versus SS identification. VGAT-positive presynaptic labeling on SS in serial FIB-SEM confirmed the morphological calls on immunostained tissue without ferrocyanide as a further check.
ocar.future_work: The methods paper positions the protocol for quantitative cortical synapse organization; the selected extract’s main methods/results narrative is truncated before full counts, so density statistics are not taken from this extract.

summaries.beginner: Inhibitory synapses are thin and easy to miss in 3D electron-microscope pictures, especially after a stain that makes membranes darker. This protocol uses a weaker stain so both excitatory and inhibitory synapses can still be told apart, and it checks the inhibitory ones with a GABA marker.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2024), Cano-Astorga and colleagues address AS/SS classification in FIB-SEM of cerebral cortex. Increasing potassium ferrocyanide, used to enhance membranes, makes PSDs thinner and SS harder to identify. They report that 0.1% ferrocyanide improves membrane contrast while preserving unequivocal AS versus SS calls, and they validate SS as GABAergic using VGAT immunocytochemistry on mouse sections processed with different ferrocyanide concentrations. Serial-section examples show VGAT-positive SS terminals.
summaries.advanced: The extract jumps from the abstract to acknowledgments and a figure of VGAT-labeled serial synapses; numeric AS/SS densities are not in the selected text. “Unequivocal” is the authors’ protocol claim under the stated chemistry, not a claim that all volume-EM pipelines should drop ferrocyanide. VGAT experiments are on fixed mouse sections; AS≈glutamate and SS≈GABA remain cortical generalizations. Frontiers editorial-board note is disclosed for an author.

plain_language_summary: Inhibitory synapses are thin and easy to miss in 3D electron-microscope pictures, especially after a stain that makes membranes darker. This protocol uses a weaker stain so both excitatory and inhibitory synapses can still be told apart, and it checks the inhibitory ones with a GABA marker.

ocar.opportunity: New microscopy modalities often lack instance labels; a model that translates appearance and segments in one network could reuse EM nuclei labels on unlabeled expansion microscopy.
ocar.challenge: Sequential translation-then-segmentation uses two independent networks, and expert 3D instance annotation is expensive.
ocar.action: Lauenburg, Lin, Zhang, dos Santos, Huang, Arganda-Carreras, Boyden, Pfister, and Wei present CySGAN in IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics (2023): a cyclic segmentation GAN with shared weights for 3D image translation and instance segmentation, trained with CycleGAN, supervised source, self-supervised, and segmentation-adversarial losses.
ocar.resolution: On 3D neuronal nuclei segmentation from annotated EM to unlabeled ExM, CySGAN outperformed pretrained generalist models, feature-level domain-adaptation models, and sequential translation-plus-segmentation baselines. The translation head can be dropped at inference, so deployment cost matches a standard 3D segmenter. They release code and NucExM, a densely annotated ExM zebrafish brain nuclei dataset.
ocar.future_work: Related-work discussion contrasts 2D semantic methods such as SUSAN and argues 3D instance segmentation plus unlabeled-domain semi-supervised losses are the distinguishing bets; numeric leaderboard scores are not in the selected extract.

summaries.beginner: A computer trained to outline cell nuclei in electron-microscope images may fail on a different kind of microscope. This method learns to both restyle the pictures and outline nuclei in one network, then throws away the restyling part when it is time to run.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE JBHI (August 2023), Lauenburg, Lin, and colleagues introduce CySGAN, unifying CycleGAN-style translation with 3D instance segmentation via weight sharing. Source supervision is on annotated EM; unlabeled ExM is used through self-supervised and segmentation-based adversarial objectives. The task is neuronal nuclei instance segmentation; CySGAN is reported to beat generalist pretrained models, feature-level adaptation, and two-network sequential baselines. NucExM, a densely annotated expansion-microscopy zebrafish brain nuclei set, is released with the code.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF extract does not include quantitative AP/F1 tables; outperformance is taken from the abstract. Domain pair is EM→ExM nuclei, not general connectomic membrane segmentation. Inference without the translation layer matches a standard segmenter only if that architecture is used. NucExM labels are for nuclei, not full neuron instances. Comparison to SUSAN is conceptual (2D semantic vs 3D instance; unlabeled-domain losses).

plain_language_summary: A computer trained to outline cell nuclei in electron-microscope images may fail on a different kind of microscope. This method learns to both restyle the pictures and outline nuclei in one network, then throws away the restyling part when it is time to run.

ocar.opportunity: Volumetric EM now yields full circuit wiring, but detailed biophysical simulations have too many parameters to reveal which ones set function.
ocar.challenge: Linear tools miss spikes, synaptic nonlinearities, and multistability, while high-dimensional GLMs are hard to fit on large connectomes.
ocar.action: Borst and Leibold, in a Journal of Neuroscience TechSights article (2023), review linear dynamical-systems analysis and matrix-reordering methods as ways to extract time constants and motifs (feedforward versus feedback) from connectivity matrices.
ocar.resolution: They argue linear algebra can predict network time constants far longer than membrane constants and can expose structural motifs only after reordering. Combined with constrained nonlinear simulations, this is presented as a practical path from connectomes to physiology.
ocar.future_work: Open problems include threshold-linear analyses not yet applied to connectomes, choice of noise models for graded neurons, and which nonlinear connectome-constrained approach (if any) becomes standard.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram is not a movie of brain activity. This viewpoint explains simple math that can reveal hidden loops and slow timescales that come from how cells are connected, not from each cell’s membrane alone.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Neuroscience (2023), Borst and Leibold review how to connect volumetric-EM connectomes to physiology without treating every biophysical parameter as essential. Linear dynamical systems can yield effective time constants from architecture; matrix reordering can distinguish feedforward from feedback organization. They contrast this with limitations of purely linear models (no multistability, ignored spike/synapse nonlinearities) and with GLMs whose inverse-link functions are unsettled for graded neurons. Cited success stories include connectome-constrained fly visual networks and Bayesian comparison of column models to connectivity.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods viewpoint, not a new dataset or circuit discovery. Recommendations are qualitative. Threshold-linear subspace methods (Curto; Santander) are noted as unused on connectomes here. “Gold standard” nonlinear approach is explicitly unsettled. Insight claims assume a well-constrained connectivity matrix and a meaningful linearized operating point.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram is not a movie of brain activity. This viewpoint explains simple math that can reveal hidden loops and slow timescales that come from how cells are connected, not from each cell’s membrane alone.

ocar.opportunity: Mitochondrial geometry in EM informs cell type and disease, but prior instance-segmentation benchmarks used tiny volumes.
ocar.challenge: Large, morphologically diverse mitochondria produce errors that small-volume metrics miss, and the original challenge metric was too kind to false positives.
ocar.action: Franco-Barranco, Lin, Jang, Wang, Shen, Yin, Fan, and many challenge participants, in IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging (2023), report the ISBI 2021 MitoEM challenge on two cortex volumes (human and rat) 1,986 times larger than previous datasets, covering 257 registrants, 14 submitting teams, and eight top methods plus organizer baselines.
ocar.resolution: Ground-truth errors were corrected after the challenge without changing the ranking. A retrospective found the original metric permissive of false positives and a poor size-based grouping of instances; a new scoring system is proposed. Several top methods beat the organizers’ baselines, but hard morphologies remain unsolved. The challenge stays open with public volumes.
ocar.future_work: Open submission and automatic evaluation are intended to continue progress on remaining morphological failure modes.

summaries.beginner: Finding every mitochondrion in a huge electron-microscope block is harder than on the tiny test cubes used before. A community challenge on human and rat cortex shows that even the best methods still fail on tricky shapes, and that the original scorecard was too easy on false alarms.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE TMI (2023), Franco-Barranco and colleagues summarize MitoEM (ISBI 2021): two large 3D EM volumes from human and rat cortex, 1,986× larger than prior mitochondria instance datasets. Of 257 registered participants, 14 teams submitted and six joined the workshop; eight top approaches plus baselines are presented. Post-challenge ground-truth fixes did not change ranking. The authors critique the original metric (false-positive permissiveness; inadequate size grouping) and propose a replacement. Substantial errors remain for challenging morphologies; data stay downloadable.
summaries.advanced: The selected extract jumps from the abstract/introduction into references, so per-team scores are not in this text. “Compared favorably to our own baselines” is qualitative here. Ranking invariance after GT correction is stated without listing the errors. Human and rat volumes should not be averaged into one accuracy. Mitochondria instance segmentation is related to, but not the same as, neuron or synapse segmentation.

plain_language_summary: Finding every mitochondrion in a huge electron-microscope block is harder than on the tiny test cubes used before. A community challenge on human and rat cortex shows that even the best methods still fail on tricky shapes, and that the original scorecard was too easy on false alarms.

ocar.opportunity: Globular bushy cells time-stamp sound, but missing 3D innervation maps have left coincidence-detection versus mixed suprathreshold-input hypotheses underconstrained.
ocar.challenge: Compartmental models need true surface areas, endbulb weights, and dendrite geometry, not schematic cartoons.
ocar.action: Spirou, Kersting, Carr, Razzaq, Alves-Pinto, Dawson, Ellisman, and Manis, on bioRxiv (2023), build volume-EM synaptic maps of auditory-nerve endbulbs onto GBCs and export reconstructions into biophysically detailed compartmental models driven by a cochlear transduction model.
ocar.resolution: Models predict either all-subthreshold endbulbs (coincidence detection) or one to two suprathreshold inputs (mixed mode). Dendrite geometry, soma size, and axon-initial-segment length are predicted to set threshold and response heterogeneity, suggesting homeostatic excitability knobs. Volume EM also revealed dendritic hubs, filaments near mitochondria, and dendrites lacking innervation.
ocar.future_work: The authors list missing cellular parameters that new experiments should supply and treat the pipeline as a template for other neuron classes; the extract’s later pages are figure supplements rather than a full limitations list.

summaries.beginner: Some cochlear-nucleus cells lock spikes to sound timing. This study measures their 3D shape and nerve endings in electron-microscope volumes, then runs those measurements in a computer model to test how the cells add up inputs.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2023), Spirou and colleagues use volume EM to specify auditory-nerve convergence, synaptic weights, and postsynaptic surface areas of globular bushy cells, then import axons, endbulbs, dendrites, somata, and axons into compartmental models driven by a standard cochlear model. Predicted innervation profiles are all-subthreshold (coincidence detection) or mixed with one to two suprathreshold endbulbs. Models also rank dendrite geometry, soma size, and AIS length as determinants of spike threshold and response diversity. New dendritic structures and uninnervated dendrites are reported.
summaries.advanced: Predictions are model outputs under stated biophysical assumptions, not in vivo GBC recordings from the same cells. The selected extract jumps into shuffled-autocorrelation supplements; quantitative convergence ratios are not copied here. Catalog method tags include volume EM, matching the paper. “Template for other neuron classes” is prospective. Co-corresponding authors Spirou and Manis are on the PDF; catalog author list omits Manis.

plain_language_summary: Some cochlear-nucleus cells lock spikes to sound timing. This study measures their 3D shape and nerve endings in electron-microscope volumes, then runs those measurements in a computer model to test how the cells add up inputs.

ocar.opportunity: Opponent inhibition is a common motif, but the fly lobula plate offers EM connectivity plus physiology to show how it is implemented across network levels.
ocar.challenge: Synapse counts badly understate inhibition if unitary inhibitory conductances are much larger, and a single-stage push–pull of huge opposing conductances would crush gain.
ocar.action: Ammer, Serbe-Kamp, Mauss, Richter, Fendl, and Borst, in Nature Neuroscience (2023), combine optogenetics, voltage and calcium imaging, connectomics, electrophysiology, and modeling of Drosophila T4/T5, LPi, and LPTC motion circuits.
ocar.resolution: A single cell type implements direction-selective, GluClα-mediated motion-opponent inhibition at three nested levels with increasing spatiotemporal scale. Inhibition balances excitation despite tenfold (to 20-fold) fewer synapses. Distributing the computation across levels is proposed to protect gain while remaining noise-resilient and feature-selective.
ocar.future_work: They generalize that most T4/T5 postsynaptic cells also get LPi input, so multilevel opponency may be a lobula-plate principle; calcium weakly reports null-direction voltage, a rectification caveat for imaging-only studies.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly motion cells are tuned to opposite directions and suppress each other. This paper shows that the same kind of push–pull happens at three successive circuit layers, and that a few strong inhibitory contacts can match many weak excitatory ones.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Neuroscience (2023), Ammer and colleagues dissect motion-opponent inhibition in the Drosophila lobula plate. Direction-selective T4/T5 inputs, inhibitory LPi neurons, and large-field LPTCs form nested opponent stages operating at increasing spatial and temporal scales. Opponent inhibition is GluClα-mediated and balanced with excitation in strength despite ~10–20× fewer inhibitory synapses, implying much larger unitary inhibitory conductances. Electrophysiology and modeling argue that spreading the computation across levels avoids the gain collapse of integrating large opposing conductances once. VS cells at the output act as flow-field selectivity filters.
summaries.advanced: Tenfold–20-fold synapse-count asymmetry is anatomical; physiological balance is inferred from combined measurements, not a single universal ratio. Calcium versus voltage discrepancy on null-direction (ND) stimulation is a major caveat for Ca²⁺ imaging. “Single cell type at all three levels” refers to the architecture they uncover, not one neuron doing every computation. Natural-scene statistics are used as functional interpretation, not a new ecology experiment in this extract.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly motion cells are tuned to opposite directions and suppress each other. This paper shows that the same kind of push–pull happens at three successive circuit layers, and that a few strong inhibitory contacts can match many weak excitatory ones.

ocar.opportunity: Same-axon, same-dendrite synapse pairs share coactivation history, so their size similarity can estimate how many distinguishable synaptic weights a circuit can store.
ocar.challenge: Signal-detection estimates of storage capacity are biased by overlapping states and outliers; Shannon clustering of non-overlapping spine-head volumes is proposed instead.
ocar.action: Samavat, Bartol, Bromer, Bowden, Hubbard, Hanka, Kuwajima, Mendenhall, Parker, Abraham, Harris, and Sejnowski, on bioRxiv (2023), define synaptic information storage capacity (SISC) on 3DEM spine-head volumes in rat hippocampus after in vivo LTP versus control.
ocar.resolution: CA1 stratum radiatum spines occupied 24 distinguishable states (4.1 bits). Dentate gyrus middle molecular layer controls occupied 5 states (2 bits), rising to 10 states (3 bits) by 30 minutes after LTP and lasting at least 2 hours, with a broader, nearly uniform occupancy of the new states.
ocar.future_work: They present SISC as a probe of plasticity in normal and diseased brains; the extract’s later pages are supplementary clustering figures rather than a separate limitations section.

summaries.beginner: Memory may live in how large each dendritic spine is. By grouping spine sizes that do not overlap, this study counts how many distinct “volume notes” hippocampal synapses can play, and finds that a learning protocol increases that number in dentate gyrus.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2023), Samavat and colleagues introduce SISC: Shannon information from non-overlapping clusters of 3DEM dendritic spine-head volumes, using same-axon/same-dendrite pairs to estimate plasticity precision. In CA1 stratum radiatum they report 24 distinguishable states (4.1 bits). Control dentate gyrus middle molecular layer spines occupy 5 states (2 bits); 30 minutes after in vivo LTP this rises to 10 states (3 bits), persisting at least 2 hours, with a more uniform spread across states. Spine-head volume is treated as correlated with other synaptic-weight measures.
summaries.advanced: Bits assume discrete non-overlapping clusters whose number depends on CV from SDSA pairs; different clustering would change capacity. CA1 versus DG comparison mixes regions and sample sizes (e.g., 288 CA1 spines in a supplement histogram; DG n’s appear in supplements for 30 min/2 h control and LTP). LTP is in vivo induction, not a demonstrated behavioral memory. SISC is not a spike-based information rate. Extract does not include a full methods recap of cluster-count algorithms beyond the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Memory may live in how large each dendritic spine is. By grouping spine sizes that do not overlap, this study counts how many distinct “volume notes” hippocampal synapses can play, and finds that a learning protocol increases that number in dentate gyrus.

ocar.opportunity: Multiple synaptic-resolution connectomes now exist, so one can ask whether small brains share topological design, not only C. elegans idiosyncrasies.
ocar.challenge: Prior work emphasized single networks; it was unclear which graph properties survive across compartments and species.
ocar.action: Zhao, Shao, Shi, He, and Gong, in IEEE/ACM Transactions on Computational Biology and Bioinformatics (2023), compare nine synaptic-resolution connectomes including C. elegans, fly larval and adult subsystems, Ciona CNS, and mouse retinal IPL on small-worldness, modules, rich clubs, weight and degree distributions, and motif significance profiles.
ocar.resolution: All networks were small-world and modular; all except the Drosophila larval visual system had rich clubs. Synaptic strengths fitted truncated power laws; degree CCDFs fitted log-normals better than power laws. Motif significance profiles placed the networks in the same superfamily.
ocar.future_work: The authors read this as formation principles within and across species; the selected extract jumps from the abstract into author biographies, so per-network tables are not in the extract.

summaries.beginner: Now that several tiny nervous systems have been mapped synapse by synapse, this paper checks whether they share the same kind of network shape. They mostly do: clustered small worlds, similar connection-strength tails, and similar little wiring motifs.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE/ACM TCBB (2023), Zhao and colleagues analyze nine synapse-level connectomes spanning C. elegans, Ciona CNS, Drosophila larval circuits (visual, olfactory, mushroom body, locomotion), adult fly optic medulla and central brain, and mouse retinal IPL. Shared properties include small-world structure and modules; rich clubs in all but the larval visual system; truncated power-law synaptic strengths; and log-normal degree CCDFs outperforming power-law fits. Significance profiles of small subgraphs assign them to one motif superfamily.
summaries.advanced: Shared statistics are not a unique developmental mechanism. “Excluding the Drosophila larval visual system” for rich clubs is an important exception. Truncated power-law versus log-normal comparisons are model-selection statements on CCDFs. Mouse IPL is a partial circuit, not a whole brain. The extract lacks numerical tables (γ, λ, motif z-scores). Catalog datasets include C. elegans and Drosophila larva, matching the paper’s core but not the full nine-network list.

plain_language_summary: Now that several tiny nervous systems have been mapped synapse by synapse, this paper checks whether they share the same kind of network shape. They mostly do: clustered small worlds, similar connection-strength tails, and similar little wiring motifs.

ocar.opportunity: The Ciona larval CNS connectome lists synapses but not whether they are excitatory, inhibitory, or modulatory, blocking circuit interpretation.
ocar.challenge: Manual synapse calling is slow; neurotransmitter identity is not obvious from EM, and synapses are rare (~1:1,000 structures).
ocar.action: Zhang, Shailja, Borba, Miao, Goebel, Ruschel, Ryan, Smith, and Manjunath, in Biological Imaging (2022), train a CNN to detect synapses in serial-section TEM patches and a multimodal model to predict neurotransmitter type, using class activation maps and comparison to in situ hybridization counts.
ocar.resolution: The workflow differentiates synapses by neurotransmitter from EM structure and predicts previously unknown Ciona neuron transmitter types. For receptor neurons, predicted VGAT-positive (16) and VAChT-positive (11) averages matched prior in situ counts better than a point-cloud registration method. The detector is meant to skip full-image search given synapse rarity.
ocar.future_work: They cannot be absolutely certain on cells without prior transmitter labels; they suggest adding cell-shape, connectivity, and segmentation features, and they note CAM-based feature analysis as supporting but not proving the calls.

summaries.beginner: A complete wiring list still hides whether each connection is a “go” or “stop” signal. This study trains a computer on electron-microscope snapshots of sea-squirt synapses to guess both where synapses are and which chemical they likely use.
summaries.intermediate: In Biological Imaging (2022), Zhang and colleagues build a deep-learning workflow for Ciona intestinalis serial-section EM. A CNN classifies image patches as synapses; a multimodal model predicts neurotransmitter type from EM plus other measurements, with CAMs highlighting structural cues. The Ciona CNS is cited as 177 neurons and 6,618 synapses. Predicted receptor-neuron VGAT (average 16) and VAChT (average 11) positives align with prior in situ hybridization better than point-cloud registration. Code is on GitHub.
summaries.advanced: Transmitter predictions for previously unlabeled cells are extrapolations; the authors say they seem reasonable given CAMs and in situ matches, not ground-truth physiology. Patch classification is not a full instance-segmented synapse census. Impact-statement neuron/synapse counts describe the published connectome, not this paper’s independent recount. Comparison to in situ is at group-count level, not identified single neurons throughout.

plain_language_summary: A complete wiring list still hides whether each connection is a “go” or “stop” signal. This study trains a computer on electron-microscope snapshots of sea-squirt synapses to guess both where synapses are and which chemical they likely use.

ocar.opportunity: A brain-wide fly neuron-to-neuron connectome lets cell classes be defined by shared connection-probability profiles rather than by anatomy first.
ocar.challenge: Grouping neurons into spatial compartments can miss non-assortative mesoscale pathways that actually carry function.
ocar.action: Mehta, Goldin, and Ascoli, in Network Neuroscience (2023), fit a stochastic block model with spectral clustering on a large Drosophila neuron-to-neuron connectome, then characterize classes with transmitters, birth times, morphology, and random-walk hub/source/destination analyses.
ocar.resolution: Connectivity-based classes captured information complementary to traditional biomarkers (mutual information). A core of interconnected dopaminergic classes is interpreted as a backbone for multisensory integration, with additional predicted pathways for circadian activity (glutamatergic motor–optic links), spatial orientation, fight-or-flight, and olfactory learning. Birth-time mapping suggested distinct growth periods for pathways.
ocar.future_work: Pathways are experimentally testable hypotheses from organized architecture, not demonstrated behaviors; the authors contrast SBM grouping with LPU/compartment analyses of the same era’s connectomes.

summaries.beginner: Instead of sorting fruit-fly neurons only by brain region, this study groups cells that wire to others in the same statistical way. The groups highlight a dopamine-rich core that may stitch senses together, plus other candidate communication routes.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Network Neuroscience (2023), Mehta, Goldin, and Ascoli cluster Drosophila neurons by stochastic block modeling so that a class shares connection-probability distributions to other classes. They then map classes onto neurotransmitters, developmental birth times, morphology, spatial embedding, and functional anatomy. Graph and random-walk analyses label hubs, sources, and destinations. They report a highly interconnected dopaminergic core as a putative multisensory backbone, glutamatergic-dominant motor–optic connections possibly related to circadian activity, and further predicted pathways for orientation, fight-or-flight, and olfactory learning. Code is linked from the paper.
summaries.advanced: Catalog year is 2022 (accepted October 2022); the article is Network Neuroscience 7(1) 2023. Functional pathway names are interpretations of connectivity plus biomarkers, not causal circuit tests. Mutual information shows complementarity, not superiority, versus traditional types. The underlying connectome is a large neuron-to-neuron resource of that period (Scheffer et al. and related projects are discussed), with all SBM caveats of resolution and completeness. “Potential synaptic circuitry” is the authors’ own framing.

plain_language_summary: Instead of sorting fruit-fly neurons only by brain region, this study groups cells that wire to others in the same statistical way. The groups highlight a dopamine-rich core that may stitch senses together, plus other candidate communication routes.

ocar.opportunity: Identified neurons compared across hemispheres and individuals can show how much wiring variation is developmental noise versus experience.
ocar.challenge: Most cell types cannot be named as single cells; the extent and timescale of single-neuron wiring variability were unknown.
ocar.action: Chou, Yang, Huang, Liou, Panganiban, Luginbuhl, Yin, Taisz, Liang, Jefferis, and Luo, in Science Advances (2022), genetically label an identified inhibitory olfactory local neuron (TC-LN), score glomerular innervation across many hemispheres, and examine EM connectomes plus mating, sex, and feeding correlates.
ocar.resolution: TC-LN showed extraordinary innervation variability (as many as 849 distinct glomerular patterns). VL2a innervation (food odor; mating-related) was sexually dimorphic, depended on female courtship experience, and correlated with food intake in mated females. Mating also changed TC-LN output onto specific local interneurons. The authors propose that this variability tunes food-odor interpretation after mating.
ocar.future_work: They ask whether other interneurons vary as much and whether variability could be a substrate for species differences; culture-density controls did not obviously change innervation variability.

summaries.beginner: Even a named fruit-fly neuron does not wire the same way in every animal. An inhibitory smell-circuit cell called TC-LN visits different odor maps depending on sex and whether a female has mated, which may change how food odors are treated.
summaries.intermediate: In Science Advances (2022), Chou and colleagues identify TC-LN, one inhibitory local interneuron per antennal lobe, confirmed in EM connectomes covering three hemispheres. Binary glomerular innervation yielded as many as 849 distinct patterns. VL2a innervation—tied to IR84a food-odor channels and mating behavior—was sexually dimorphic, modulated by female courtship experience, and correlated with food intake in mated females. Mating also affected TC-LN outputs onto specific LNs. Discussion proposes TC-LN as a switch in a dynamic VL2a local connectome that modulates feeding after mating.
summaries.advanced: 849 is a count of observed binary innervation patterns, not a proof of 849 computational types. Correlation with food intake is not a demonstrated causal feeding circuit. EM confirmation is one TC-LN per lobe in the examined datasets, while variability statistics come from light-level labeling. GAD1-GAL80 intersection labeling had rare exceptions. Catalog organism tags are empty; the paper is Drosophila olfaction.

plain_language_summary: Even a named fruit-fly neuron does not wire the same way in every animal. An inhibitory smell-circuit cell called TC-LN visits different odor maps depending on sex and whether a female has mated, which may change how food odors are treated.

ocar.opportunity: Voxel segmentations of terabyte EM volumes need skeletons before morphology and synapses can be quantified in one environment.
ocar.challenge: Existing skeletonization and analysis tools are split across languages; sparse, distributed skeletonization on cloud segmentations is awkward.
ocar.action: Wu, Turner, Bae, Vishwanathan, and Seung present RealNeuralNetworks.jl in Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2022), a Julia package for sparse skeletonization, morphological metrics, NBLAST clustering, and synaptic connectivity analysis, demonstrated on a large zebrafish segmentation with Google Cloud.
ocar.resolution: They illustrate distributed skeletonization, NBLAST-based neuron clustering, and combining morphological similarity with synaptic connectivity. The package is argued to be suitable for terabyte-scale EM segmentations, with code, BigArrays.jl, and notebooks released on GitHub.
ocar.future_work: The conclusion hopes the tool is useful for other connectomics projects; no independent benchmark table is in the selected extract.

summaries.beginner: Computers that color in neurons still leave a blob, not a stick-figure skeleton. This Julia toolbox turns huge electron-microscope segmentations into skeletons you can measure and compare, shown on a zebrafish dataset in the cloud.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2022), Wu, Turner, Bae, Vishwanathan, and Seung describe RealNeuralNetworks.jl for efficient sparse skeletonization, morphology, and synaptic connectivity in Julia.
